result: SLI and SAXS show quantitative agreement for in-plane fiber orientations, including crossing fibers. In the vervet brain, the mean angular difference is ~0.017° (median absolute ~4.1°) for single fiber orientations and ~0.316° (median absolute ~5.6°) for two fiber orientations. The 2D fiber orientations from SAXS corresponded very well to those from SLI.
evaluation: Claims C3, C29, C31, C32, C55, and C105 collectively demonstrate strong quantitative agreement between SLI and SAXS for in-plane fiber orientations. The small angular differences (median absolute differences of ~4-6°) and distributions centered around zero provide robust evidence. The findings are supported by detailed experimental data in Figures 3-4.

result: dMRI shows high agreement with SAXS for main fiber orientations, with median angular differences of 14.4° over all voxels (9.1° for voxels with FA>0.2). In the corona radiata, dMRI and SAXS have median angular differences of 5.6° and 6.0° for first and second orientations, respectively. In the corpus callosum, the median angular difference is 5.7°.
evaluation: Claims C4, C33-C38 demonstrate strong agreement between dMRI and SAXS for primary fiber orientations, supported by quantitative metrics (dot product approximating unity, small angular differences). The data show dMRI can accurately resolve multiple fiber orientations per voxel in white matter, including crossing fibers in the corona radiata. Evidence is provided in Figure 5 and supplements.

result: dMRI detects spurious secondary fiber orientations in regions where SAXS and SLI show homogeneous fiber populations. In the corpus callosum, dMRI shows secondary fiber populations perpendicular to the main orientation, which are not observed by SAXS or SLI. Quantitatively, dMRI detected secondary orientations in 64% of voxels versus 31% for SAXS in the posterior section (104% increase), and 40% increase in the anterior section.
evaluation: Claims C39-C43, C107-C108 document a systematic discrepancy between dMRI and SAXS/SLI regarding secondary fiber orientations. The quantitative data (104% and 40% increases) and confirmation by high-resolution SLI (C40) provide strong evidence. The authors appropriately identify this as a known artifact (C107) and suggest solutions (C108). Evidence is provided in Figure 5 and supplements.

result: SAXS and dMRI confirm theoretical predictions that SLI peak distance decreases with increasing fiber inclination. Out-of-plane inclination angles from dMRI highly agree with those from 3D-sSAXS. However, quantification of fiber inclination based on SLI peak distance alone is challenging, especially for fibers with inclinations up to 60°, though regions with steep fibers (>70°) can be clearly identified.
evaluation: Claims C5, C44-C52, C116-C117 demonstrate experimental validation of theoretical predictions about SLI through-plane fiber orientation determination. The scatter plots (Figure 6G) confirm the predicted relationship, though with limitations for moderate inclinations. The high agreement between dMRI and SAXS for out-of-plane angles (C46) strengthens the validation. The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (C116).

result: SLI provides information about 3D fiber orientations but is limited in quantifying out-of-plane angles, especially in regions with crossing fibers and inclined crossing fibers.
evaluation: Claims C56, C57, and C118 accurately characterize the capabilities and limitations of SLI for 3D fiber orientation determination. The conclusions are supported by the experimental validation using SAXS and dMRI as references (Figure 6). The limitations are appropriately documented and acknowledged.

result: Combined SAXS and SLI measurements can provide a reliable reference (potential gold standard) for axonal orientation maps with high resolution and specificity. Both methods can reliably resolve crossing fiber orientations and serve as validation tools for dMRI-derived fiber orientations.
evaluation: Claims C6, C19, C58, C87, C88, C102, and C134 represent the main conclusion of the study. The conclusion is well-supported by the cross-validation results showing high agreement between methods (C3, C29-C32, C55, C105) and their complementary strengths. The characterization as 'potential' or 'towards' a gold standard is appropriately cautious.

result: For in-plane fibers, both SLI and SAXS show strongest signal perpendicular to fiber orientation with azimuthal peaks 180° apart. For crossing fibers, each bundle produces two peaks 180° apart. For partly out-of-plane fibers, SAXS peaks remain 180° apart but become less pronounced, while SLI peak distance decreases with increasing inclination. For highly out-of-plane fibers, both methods show radially symmetric patterns without significant peaks.
evaluation: Claims C20-C25 describe the fundamental signal characteristics of SLI and SAXS for different fiber configurations. These observations are well-documented in Figure 2 with representative scattering patterns and azimuthal profiles. The findings are consistent with the physical principles of both methods and provide the foundation for fiber orientation determination.

result: dMRI has limited spatial resolution (typically a few hundred micrometers in post-mortem human brains) that is insufficient to resolve individual nerve fibers. Isolating the anisotropic signal from myelinated axons is challenging, and voxels may contain hundreds of fibers with complicated geometries including crossings.
evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C9 accurately describe established limitations of dMRI. These statements are supported by citations (C7) and represent well-known challenges in the field. They provide important context for the validation study.

result: SAXS provides myelinated nerve fiber orientations by studying anisotropy of myelin diffraction peaks generated by interaction with the layered myelin sheath structure. SAXS can be tomographic and 3D-sSAXS can provide 3D distributions of axon orientations in tissue sections. SAXS can resolve crossing nerve fiber populations with resolutions of tens of micrometers.
evaluation: Claims C2, C10-C14 describe the principles and capabilities of SAXS, supported by citations to prior work and Figure 1. These statements accurately represent established knowledge about SAXS and provide necessary background for the study.

result: Light scattering can reveal crossing nerve fiber orientations as it is sensitive to directional arrangements of myelinated axons. SLI can reliably reconstruct up to three in-plane fiber orientations per pixel with accuracy of ±2.4° and micrometer-scale in-plane resolution.
evaluation: Claims C15-C18 describe the principles and capabilities of SLI, supported by citations to prior work and Figure 1. These statements accurately represent established knowledge about SLI and provide necessary background for the study.

result: In the corona radiata, fibers of the corpus callosum fan out while crossing the ascending internal/external capsule.
evaluation: Claim C30 describes a specific anatomical observation from the experimental data, supported by Figure 3. This finding demonstrates the ability of both SLI and SAXS to resolve complex fiber architecture.

result: The broadly distributed SLI peak distances in the cingulum may be due to difficulty determining peak distance in regions with highly inclined fibers. The cingulate gyrus contains a transverse in-plane fiber bundle in addition to the highly inclined cingulum bundle, explaining large SLI peak distances in some regions.
evaluation: Claims C53-C54 provide interpretations of experimental observations supported by Figure 6 and dMRI orientation distribution functions. The explanations are reasonable and consistent with the data, though they represent inferences rather than direct measurements.

result: SAXS and SLI have fundamental differences in physical principles (X-ray vs. visible light wavelengths, myelin periodicity vs. axonal arrangement) but share important features: both are orientation-specific methods that directly probe fiber orientation, produce similar azimuthal profiles for in-plane fibers, can image similarly-prepared sections without staining, and are non-destructive. SAXS works on individual fibers and allows measurements irrespective of thickness, while SLI requires multiple fibers and yields higher in-plane resolution without raster-scanning.
evaluation: Claims C89-C104 provide a comprehensive comparison of SAXS and SLI methodologies. The statements are supported by citations, established physical principles, and the experimental setup described in the Methods. This comparison is important for understanding the complementary nature of the techniques.

result: Regions with low dot product between dMRI and SAXS are regions with two strong crossing fiber populations, so correspondence of primary orientation is expectedly low.
evaluation: Claim C106 provides a reasonable interpretation of the experimental data supported by Figure 5. The explanation is consistent with the methodology where primary orientation correspondence would be low in regions with strong crossing fibers.

result: The SAXS/SLI section was 80 μm thick compared to 200 μm dMRI voxels, meaning dMRI voxels might contain additional fiber orientations. Results were obtained using a single dMRI analysis method (MRtrix3 dwi2response and dwi2fod), and other methods might yield different results. Results from two sections of a single specimen should be interpreted with caution.
evaluation: Claims C109-C113 appropriately acknowledge important methodological limitations and caveats. These statements demonstrate scientific rigor in interpretation and are factually accurate regarding the experimental design.

result: Only fiber orientations were compared, not fiber dispersion/orientation distributions. It would be possible to derive fiber dispersion information from SLI and SAXS using a process similar to constrained spherical deconvolution in dMRI, though this has not been implemented yet.
evaluation: Claims C114-C115 accurately describe the scope of the current study and suggest potential future developments. The suggestion for deriving fiber dispersion is reasonable speculation based on established methods in dMRI.

result: Machine learning models trained on simulated data sets could help improve interpretation of measured scattering patterns from SLI and yield more reliable estimates.
evaluation: Claim C119 is a suggestion for future improvement supported by a citation. While reasonable, this represents speculation about potential future developments rather than a finding of the current study. The feasibility and effectiveness of this approach remain to be demonstrated.

result: Different resolutions of SLI, SAXS, and dMRI should be considered when interpreting comparative studies. dMRI voxels contain more than double the fiber layers of SAXS/SLI sections. Fiber orientations occurring in both SAXS/SLI and dMRI can be considered reliable given different contrast mechanisms. dMRI could complement SLI measurements to improve interpretation of through-plane fiber orientations.
evaluation: Claims C120-C123 provide important considerations for interpreting the comparative results and suggest future applications. The statements are factually accurate regarding the experimental design (C121) and provide reasonable inferences about reliability (C122) and future applications (C123).

result: Image registration accuracy is crucial for cross-validation quality. The relatively thick sections (60-80 μm) were not prone to significant non-linear deformations, and linear transformations were sufficient. Some individual voxels might not be sufficiently well aligned, so inter-method differences can be considered as an upper bound.
evaluation: Claims C124-C128 address important methodological considerations regarding image registration. The statements are supported by the registration quality shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and represent appropriate acknowledgment of potential limitations.

result: The cross-validation study focused on in-plane (single or crossing) and through-plane (single) fiber populations. Confident assessment of highly inclined crossing fibers is not possible because they yield flat azimuthal profiles with multiple small peaks. In-plane orientations in regions with highly inclined fibers are naturally less reliable.
evaluation: Claims C129-C132 appropriately define the scope and limitations of the study. The statements are supported by experimental observations (Figure 2) and represent appropriate scientific caution about the reliability of measurements in challenging regions.

result: The study focused on comparison and cross-validation rather than combining measurement results. A combined analysis would greatly enhance accuracy and reliability of brain connectivity maps, but faces challenges: dMRI provides volumetric information while SLI requires thin sections, and SAXS tensor tomography reconstruction of crossing fibers in volumes has only been demonstrated in sections. Future developments in robust tomographic reconstruction and machine learning approaches could enable full combination of methods and improve dMRI and in-vivo applications.
evaluation: Claims C133-C140 accurately describe the scope of the current study (C133) and discuss future directions. While the potential benefits of combined analysis are reasonable (C134), the specific future developments (C137, C139, C140) represent speculation. The challenges identified (C135-C136) are factually accurate.

result: Various existing methods for identifying fiber orientations have limitations: histological staining has limitations in densely packed white matter and causes tissue deformation; serial electron microscopy requires small samples and complex preparation; tissue clearing causes deformation; structure tensor analysis requires kernels that limit resolution; polarization microscopy yields only single fiber orientations and has challenges with crossing fibers and out-of-plane angles; all sectioning techniques require accurate registration and tractography; tracer studies are limited to specific pathways and animal brains.
evaluation: Claims C59-C83 provide a comprehensive review of existing methods and their limitations, supported by numerous citations. These statements accurately represent established knowledge in the field and provide important context for the study. The characterizations of limitations are well-documented in the cited literature.

result: Multiple studies reveal that dMRI tractography often yields false-positive fiber tracts, dMRI orientations differ up to 20° for secondary fiber orientations, and fiber crossings at angles smaller than 60° cannot be resolved.
evaluation: Claims C84-C86 summarize established limitations of dMRI from prior validation studies, supported by citations. These statements provide important context for the need for validation methods like SAXS and SLI.

result: The study used vervet monkey brain (2.4-year-old male) and human brain (66-year-old female) samples with appropriate ethical approvals. SLI measurements used an LED display with 128×128 RGB-LEDs and CCD camera, yielding 3.0 μm/px in-plane resolution. 3D-sSAXS was performed at Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource with 15 keV photon energy, 100-150 μm beam diameter. dMRI was performed on a Bruker 11.7T scanner at 200 μm isotropic voxels.
evaluation: Claims C141-C149 provide factual descriptions of the experimental materials and methods. These statements are straightforward descriptions of the experimental setup and are internally consistent with the results presented.
